King Charles heads to Caribbean as calls for slavery reparations grow

Reuters

27 October, 2026 01:00 pm IST

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

By Michael Holden LONDON, Oct 27 (Reuters) – King Charles heads to the Caribbean this week on a tour which comes against the backdrop of increasingly vocal demands from the region that Britain pays reparations for its role in the slave trade.

Charles and his wife Queen Camilla will first visit the Bahamas and Guyana, before heading to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), the biennial get-together of the international organisation which he heads. The tour runs from October 27 to November 4.

At a previous meeting in 2022 of the leaders of the Commonwealth — a group of 56 nations which were mainly former British colonies — Charles expressed deep personal sorrow over slavery, and the issue is certain to be prominent once again.

Show Full Article

Last month, CARICOM, the Caribbean Community, a group of 23 member and associate member states which includes the Bahamas, Barbados and Jamaica, said it would push for reparations to be on the CHOGM agenda.

“The Caribbean has consistently asserted that reparations is fundamentally about justice,” CARICOM’s Secretary-General Carla Barnett said in a speech last month.

“It is about recognition, accountability and transformation, and about building a just and equitable future for the descendants of those who, as the chattel of colonial owners, endured untold suffering, loss of life and freedom.”

While Buckingham Palace has said the monarch would not shy away from Britain’s involvement in the transatlantic slave trade during his tour, he would not formally apologise for it as some have wanted, in keeping with British government policy which also excludes making any financial reparations.

“It is important to note here the work his majesty himself has done over many years both to acknowledge the wrongs of the past and to find creative ways to right inequalities that endure,” a palace spokesperson said.

Shirley Botchwey, the secretary-general of the Commonwealth, which encompasses some 2.7 billion people, said last week the time had come for discussions about reparations, be they financial or in some other form such as the return of artefacts.

As for an apology from the king, who remains the head of state of a number of Caribbean nations including both the Bahamas and Antigua and Barbuda, she told Sky News: “It wouldn’t hurt to have that.”

From the 15th to the 19th century, at least 12.5 million Africans were abducted and sold into slavery by European merchants, with Britain responsible for transporting an estimated 3.2 million people, making it the second most active European nation after Portugal.

(Reporting by Michael Holden; Editing by Xevi Fontdegloria)

Indian media groups decry Modi’s privacy law in court, say newsrooms face shutdown risk

Reuters

27 October, 2026 01:00 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

By Aditya Kalra NEW DELHI, Oct 27 (Reuters) – The Indian government’s privacy law, which would require journalists to seek consent from people they write about, amounted to pre-censorship and could lead to newsrooms shutting down, media groups told the Supreme Court on Tuesday, starting the most high-profile challenge against the legislation.

The lawsuit comes amid accusations of declining press freedom in India since Prime Minister Narendra Modi took office in 2014. Critics say many mainstream media outlets have not done enough to scrutinise Modi’s government, which has denied such allegations and says it respects press freedom.

A group of 21 news publishers, including companies owned by billionaires Mukesh Ambani and Gautam Adani, has challenged the privacy law, arguing it would trample upon investigative work and allow New Delhi to identify journalists’ sources, Reuters reported on Monday.

Show Full Article

“It is changing the whole concept of what is news,” Madhavi Goradia Divan, the lawyer for Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA) told the judges.

“Newsrooms will shut down, if we have to ask for permission…it’s then a complete regime of pre-censorship.”

The lawsuit is the most high-profile challenge to Modi’s privacy law. Until now, only free speech activists and a group of smaller news outlets had challenged it.

The Supreme Court posted the case for next month.

BIG MEDIA GROUPS VS MODI

Media companies received assurances in an August meeting with the government that the law would protect press freedom, but not having a written carve-out for journalists like in the European Union, Singapore and Britain was alarming, the news publishers said in a filing earlier this month.

The publishers are demanding that most of the law’s contentious provisions, which kick in from May 2027, should be quashed. They say the law could also force publishers to erase stories and give powers to government to demand information from publishers that could expose reporters’ sources.

DNPA, the group which has challenged Modi’s government, counts as members Ambani’s Network18, Adani’s NDTV and other marquee media groups including the Indian Express and Times Internet, which is part of the Times of India group, publisher of India’s largest-selling English-language daily.

Divan said during the hearing that earlier versions of the law excluded journalists, but the final one did not.

(Reporting by Aditya Kalra; Editing by Thomas Derpinghaus and Raju Gopalakrishnan)
